title: Git and GitHub
summary: Build a precise mental model of snapshots, branches, merges, remotes, pull requests, and automated checks without treating Git as a list of magic commands.
learningOutcomes: Explain Git as a graph of snapshots and names.
Move work safely from working tree to commit to remote.
Use pull requests and CI as evidence gates.

heroVisual.title: From local change to deployed main
heroVisual.caption: Every transition has evidence and ownership.

nodes.label: Working tree
nodes.detail: Files currently present on the computer.

nodes.label: Index
nodes.detail: The exact next snapshot selected for commit.

nodes.label: Commit
nodes.detail: An immutable snapshot plus parent link and metadata.

nodes.label: Branch
nodes.detail: A movable name pointing to a commit.

nodes.label: Remote
nodes.detail: Another repository with its own references.

nodes.label: Pull request
nodes.detail: A hosted review and integration proposal.

nodes.label: Workflow

sections.title: 1. Git stores snapshots connected as a graph
sections.summary: Commits are durable nodes; branches are movable labels.

blocks.text: A Git commit records a project snapshot, metadata, and one or more parent commits. The parent links form a directed history graph. A branch such as main is not a container of files; it is a reference that moves to the newest commit in that line of work.

items.title: Commit
items.summary: Immutable project snapshot and history node.

items.title: Branch
items.whenToUse: Develop an isolated line of work or mark an authoritative line.

items.title: Tag
items.summary: Usually an immovable human-readable name for a specific commit.

blocks.title: HEAD
blocks.body: The reference that identifies the currently checked-out commit or branch, which determines where the next commit advances.

visual.title: A small commit graph
visual.caption: Names move; committed snapshots do not.

nodes.label: M
nodes.detail: A merge joins both parent histories.

sections.title: 2. A change moves through explicit local states
sections.summary: The staging area lets one working directory produce a precise commit.

items.title: Edit the working tree
items.explanation: Create, modify, rename, or remove files.
items.result: Git can show the difference from the selected commit.

items.title: Inspect
items.explanation: Use status and diff before selecting changes.
items.result: Unexpected files or secrets are caught early.

items.title: Stage intentionally
items.explanation: Add the exact changes that belong in the next snapshot.
items.result: The index represents the proposed commit.

items.title: Review the staged diff
items.explanation: Read what will be committed, not only what exists in the editor.

items.title: Commit
items.explanation: Record the staged snapshot with a message explaining the change.
items.result: The branch reference advances to the new commit.

blocks.code:
git status
git diff
git add src/search.ts tests/search.test.ts
git diff --staged
git commit -m "feat: add typo-tolerant topic search"
blocks.explanation: This sequence inspects before and after staging, then records one coherent behavior change.

blocks.title: Staging is not backup
blocks.body: Uncommitted files can still be lost. Commits provide durable local history; pushing creates another repository copy, but neither replaces an appropriate backup strategy for all data.

sections.title: 3. Branches isolate lines of work; integration combines them
sections.summary: Choose merge or rebase based on the history contract, then verify the result.

rows: Merge
Creates or fast-forwards to a history containing both lines.
A true merge commit preserves both parent lines.
Rebase
Replays commits onto a new parent.
Commit identities change; do not casually rewrite shared history.
Cherry-pick
Applies the change represented by selected commits.
Creates new commits and can duplicate logical changes.
Revert
Creates a new commit that inverses an earlier change.
Preserves published history while undoing effect.
blocks.caption: History operations

blocks.title: Conflicts are competing edits, not Git failure
blocks.body: Resolve by understanding the intended final behavior, editing the combined result, running checks, and reviewing the complete diff.

items: Update from the target branch before final review.
Resolve behavior, not just conflict markers.
Run focused and regression checks after integration.
Never force-push shared authoritative history without an explicit recovery plan.

sections.title: 4. Remotes synchronize repositories, not folders
sections.summary: Fetch updates knowledge; push requests a reference update.

blocks.code:
git fetch origin
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git push origin feature/search
blocks.explanation: Fetch downloads remote objects and references without changing the current branch. Push asks the remote to advance a named reference.

rows: origin
A conventional remote name; it is not inherently special.
origin/main
A local remote-tracking reference representing the last fetched main state.
main
A local branch reference.
upstream
The branch a local branch is configured to compare with and commonly push/pull against.
blocks.caption: Local and remote names are separate references

blocks.title: Pull is a combined operation
blocks.body: Depending on configuration, git pull fetches and then merges or rebases. Use fetch plus an explicit integration command when you need to review before changing the current branch.

sections.title: 5. GitHub adds collaboration and policy around Git
sections.summary: Pull requests, reviews, protections, issues, and releases are hosted workflow features.

items.title: Push a branch
items.explanation: Publish the proposed commits to the remote.
items.result: Others and automation can inspect the exact head commit.

items.title: Open a pull request
items.explanation: Describe purpose, scope, verification, and risk.

items.title: Run checks
items.explanation: Build, lint, test, security, and policy workflows evaluate the head commit.
items.result: Evidence is attached to the proposal.

items.title: Review the diff
items.explanation: Humans evaluate correctness, maintainability, UX, and omissions.

items.title: Integrate
items.explanation: Merge, squash, or rebase according to repository policy.

items.title: Deploy or release
items.explanation: A workflow packages or publishes the verified target state.

blocks.title: A pull request is not part of core Git
blocks.body: It is a GitHub collaboration object that compares branches and coordinates discussion, checks, approvals, and integration.

items: Body states why, what changed, how verified, and remaining risk.
No secrets, generated noise, or unrelated refactors appear in the diff.
Required checks refer to the exact head commit.

sections.title: 6. GitHub Actions turns repository events into repeatable evidence
sections.summary: A workflow is code that runs under declared permissions and triggers.

blocks.code:
name: Verify

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm check
blocks.explanation: The workflow uses explicit triggers, least-needed permissions, pinned major action lines, and a deterministic lockfile install.

items.title: Continuous integration
items.summary: Checks every proposed change against the same commands.
items.whenToUse: Build, test, lint, schema, and policy validation.

items.title: Continuous delivery
items.summary: Produces a deployable artifact after verification.

items.title: Continuous deployment
items.whenToUse: Use when rollback and operational controls are mature.

blocks.title: Workflow code is privileged automation
blocks.body: Review third-party actions, pin supported versions or immutable commits according to policy, minimize permissions, protect secrets, and treat untrusted pull-request input carefully.

sections.title: 7. Recover with evidence instead of panic
sections.summary: Most mistakes are easier to fix when published history is preserved.

rows: Uncommitted file changed incorrectly
Inspect diff; restore only the intended path after confirming no needed work is lost.
Wrong changes staged
Unstage the path while keeping the working-tree edit.
Local commit message or content wrong and unpublished
Amend if no one else depends on that commit.
Published change must be undone
Create a revert commit and verify the resulting behavior.
Secret committed
Revoke or rotate immediately, then follow history-removal policy; deleting one commit is not enough.
Branch deleted
Use reflog or known commit identifiers before objects are pruned.
blocks.caption: Recovery starts by identifying the state and publication boundary

blocks.title: Do not run destructive commands from memory
blocks.body: Before reset, clean, restore, force push, or history rewriting, inspect status, diff, log, remotes, and the exact command semantics.

items: State the desired final commit graph.
Create a safety branch or tag when recovery risk is high.
Verify the original behavior and repository status afterward.

glossary.definition: A Git object database and references representing project history, usually with a working tree.
The staging area containing the exact snapshot proposed for the next commit.
An immutable snapshot with metadata and parent link or links.
A movable reference that commonly points to the newest commit in a line of work.
A named connection to another Git repository and its tracked references.
A GitHub collaboration proposal to review and integrate one branch into another.
